L2079@P48: LEMAN-BAIKAL: REMOTE SENSING OF LAKES USING AN ULTRALIGHT PLANE
L2080@P48: Y. Akhtman, D. Constantin, M. Rehak and V. Nouchi, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
L2081@P48: G. Shinkareva, Lomonosov Moscow State University, Moscow, Russian Federation

L2085@P48: F. Duruisseau and N. Huret, Laboratoire de Physique et Chimie de l’Environnement, CNRS and Université d’Orléans, Orléans, France
L2086@P48: Abstract : The Leman-Baikal project constitutes an international Swiss- Russian collaborative research initiative in the
L2087@P48: field of physical limnology. The three-year framework involves the development and deployment of a novel multispectral and hyperspectral remote sensing platform optimised for the sensing of land and water surfaces from an ultralight aircraft. In this paper
L2088@P48: we discuss the developed remote sensing methodology and the initial obtained results.
L2089@P48: IV. Session wed-o-1-a : Imaging spectroscopy for UAVs : innovation of sensors and applications
L2090@P48: DEVELOPMENT OF LIGHTWEIGHT HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGING SYSTEM FOR UAV OBSERVATION
L2091@P48: Kuniaki Uto, Haruyuki Seki, Genya Saito and Yukio Kosugi
L2092@P48: Interdisciplinary Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Japan
L2093@P48: Abstract : To acquire accurate, real-time hyperspectral images with high spatial resolution, we develop two types of lowcost, lightweight Whisk broom hyperspectral sensors that can be loaded onto lightweight unmanned autonomous vehicle (UAV)
L2094@P48: platforms. A system is composed of two Mini- Spectrometers, a polygon mirror, references for sensor calibration, a GPS sensor,
L2095@P48: a data logger and a power supply. The acquisition of images with high spatial resolution is realized by a ground scanning along
L2096@P48: a direction perpendicular to the flight direction based on the polygon mirror. To cope with the unstable illumination condition
L2097@P48: caused by the low-altitude observation, skylight radiation and dark current are acquired in real-time by the scanning structure.
L2098@P48: Another system is composed of 2D optical fiber array connected to eight Mini- Spectrometers and a telephoto lens, a convex lens,
L2099@P48: a micro mirror, a GPS sensor, a data logger and a power supply. The acquisition of images is realized by a ground scanning based
L2100@P48: on the rotation of the micro mirror.
L2101@P48: LINEAR VARIABLE FILTERS – A CAMERA SYSTEM REQUIREMENT ANALYSIS FOR HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGING
L2102@P48: SENSORS ONBOARD SMALL REMOTELY PILOTED AIRCRAFT SYSTEMS
L2103@P48: Philippe Serruys, Aleksandra Sima and Stefan Livens, Bavo Delauré,
L2104@P48: Flemish Institute for Technological Research - VITO NV, Mol, Belgium
L2105@P48: Klaas Tack, Bert Geelen and Andy Lambrechts, IMEC, Leuven, Belgium
L2106@P48: Abstract : Improving the spectral detail of earth observation imaging from Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS)
L2107@P48: can greatly expand its potential for use in vegetation monitoring and specifically in precision agriculture. Spatially variable interference filters which can be placed very close to the image sensor offer an excellent opportunity for reducing the size, mass and
L2108@P48: complexity of hyperspectral imagers, allowing them to be mounted onboard small RPAS. Recent advances in filter deposition
L2109@P48: techniques allow to directly deposit interference filters on an image sensor. The monolithic integration of optical hyperspectral
L2110@P48: filters on top of a standard CMOS image sensor has been demonstrated by IMEC. Compared to the more conventional deposition
L2111@P48: of filters onto an external glass substrate, this new approach offers advantages in terms of cost, alignment accuracy, straylight , etc..
L2112@P48: A hyperspectral camera prototype compatible with small RPAS has been developed by VITO to demonstrate the potential of LVF-based compact spectral camera’s. Whereas application of the filter technology offers major advantages for RPAS
L2113@P48: systems, it still faces some important challenges. The prototype system specifications need to fit a fixed wing RPAS platform that is
L2114@P48: able to cover several km2 in a single flight with hyperspectral geo-information. It remains challenging to make a sufficiently compact camera system, achieve precise spectral band registration, handle the amount of data to be processed and cope with limited
L2115@P48: integration times possible during acquisition.

L2120@P49: COMBINING HYPERSPECTRAL UAV AND MULTISPECTRAL FORMOSAT-2 IMAGERY FOR PRECISION AGRICULTURE APPLICATIONS
L2121@P49: C.M. Gevaert and J.Tang,Department of Physical Geography and Ecosystem Science, Lund University, Sweden
L2122@P49: F.J. García-Haro, Department of Earth Physics and Thermodynamics, University of Valencia, Dr. Moliner, Valencia, Spain
L2123@P49: J. Suomalainen and L. Kooistra, Laboratory of Geo-Information Science and Remote Sensing, Wageningen University, the Netherlands
L2124@P49: Abstract : Remote sensing is a key tool for precision agriculture applications as it is capable of capturing spatial and
L2125@P49: temporal variations in crop status. However, satellites often have an inadequate spatial resolution for precision agriculture applications. High-resolution Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) imagery can be obtained at flexible dates, but operational costs may limit
L2126@P49: the collection frequency. The current study utilizes data fusion to create a dataset which benefits from the temporal resolution
L2127@P49: of Formosat-2 imagery and the spatial resolution of UAV imagery with the purpose of monitoring crop growth in a potato field.
L2128@P49: The correlation of the Weighted Difference Vegetation Index (WDVI) from fused imagery to measured crop indicators at field
L2129@P49: level and added value of the enhanced spatial and temporal resolution are discussed. The results of the STARFM method were
L2130@P49: restrained by the requirement of same-day base imagery. However, the unmixing-based method provided a high correlation to the
L2131@P49: field data and accurately captured the WDVI temporal variation at field level (r=0.969).
L2132@P49: HIGH SPATIAL AND SPECTRAL REMOTE SENSING FOR DETAILED MAPPING OF POTATO PLANT PARAMETERS
L2133@P49: S.Delalieux, D. Raymaekers and K. Nackaerts, VITO – Teledetection and Earth Observation Processes, Belgium
L2134@P49: E. Honkavaara, Finnish Geodetic Institute, Finland
L2135@P49: J. Soukkamäki, Rikola Ltd., Finland
L2136@P49: J. Van Den Borne, Van Den Borne Aardappelen, The Netherlands
L2137@P49: Abstract : This preliminary study shows the potential of highly flexible drones and hyperspectral technology to make
L2138@P49: detailed chlorophyll maps of an experimental potato field. A novel, innovative hyperspectral frame camera (Rikola Ltd) was
L2139@P49: employed to gather the spectral information (24 bands) at 5 cm spatial resolution. A first challenge therefore was to set- up a
L2140@P49: dedicated preprocessing chain for the images coming from this novel sensor. Coregistration of the images was successful resulting in an image displacement of only 1-2 pixels. The chlorophyll map created from the Rikola data corresponded well to the field
L2141@P49: measurements. R2 values of 0.70 were found for a linear relation between the averaged field chlorophyll measurements and the
L2142@P49: mean of the (R780- R550)/(R780+R550) index calculated for all vegetated Rikola pixels within an experimental potato cultivar
L2143@P49: plot. These chlorophyll maps which are directly linked to the vegetation status of the crops can be used by the farmer for better
L2144@P49: management decision making.
L2145@P49: UAV: A MULTIDISCIPLINARY TOOL TO ACCESS EXTREME ENVIROMENTS
L2146@P49: Alessandro Iarocci and Giovanni Romeo, Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia
L2147@P49: Adriano Mazzini, University of Oslo
L2148@P49: Giuseppe Di Stefano and Paolo Benedetti, Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia
L2149@P49: Abstract : In the recent years UAV have become an important tool for monitoring and sampling activities in a wide
L2150@P49: range of applications. Last December an UAV was used for the first time to survey the Lusi volcano (Indonesia). The aim was to
L2151@P49: take mud and gas samples, aerial photographs, videos and contact temperature measurements.
L2152@P49: Two different prototypes of remote controlled gas containers were available; in particular one prototype is a real-time
L2153@P49: telemetry and gas sampling system that returns to the ground station sensors and positioning data and receives and executes
L2154@P49: commands for the gas sampling.
L2155@P49: Another important application consists to equip the UA V with hyperspectral cameras and develop appropriate electronics in order to permit the ground station to have also a preview of the hyperspectral images during the survey.

L2161@P50: AN INTRODUCTION TO SPECTRAL GRAPH TECHNIQUES FOR THE ANALYSIS OF HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE DATA
L2162@P50: David Gillisa, Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC, USA
L2163@P50: David Messinger, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, USA
L2164@P50: Abstract : Two of the biggest challenges in analyzing HyperSpectral Image (HSI) data are that, first, the data is very
L2165@P50: high- dimensional, and secondly, by its very nature, HSI contains both spatial and spectral information. In order to make full use
L2166@P50: of this information, models and algorithms should incorporate both aspects of the data; unfortunately, this is a decidedly nontrivial problem. In recent years, spectral graph theory (including manifold learning) has proven to be a very successful technique
L2167@P50: for analyzing high-dimensional data sets. Given the highly abstract nature of graphs, many of these techniques are easily applied
L2168@P50: to HSI data; moreover, by carefully choosing how the graph is constructed, both the spatial and spectral nature of the data can be
L2169@P50: included in the model. In this note, we present a general background overview of spectral graph theory, with an emphasis on how
L2170@P50: it can be used to analyze HSI data (in particular, to perform nonlinear dimensionality reduction as well as segmentation and classification). We include examples from real-world data, and also point out some of the issues (such as computational complexity
L2171@P50: and storage requirements) that need to be addressed.
L2172@P50: SPATIAL CONTEXT DRIVEN MANIFOLD LEARNING FOR HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE
L2173@P50: Y. Zhang, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Houston
L2174@P50: H.L. Yang, School of Civil Engineering, Purdue University, US
L2175@P50: D. Lunga, Meraka Institute, Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, South Africa
L2176@P50: S. Prasad, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Houston
L2177@P50: M. Crawford, School of Civil Engineering, Purdue University, US
L2178@P50: Abstract : Manifold learning techniques have been demonstrated to be successful in representing spectral signatures in
L2179@P50: hyperspectral images, which consist of spectral features with very subtle differences and often spatially induced disjoint classes
L2180@P50: whose neighborhood relations are difficult to capture using traditional graph based embedding techniques. Robust parameter
L2181@P50: estimation is a challenge in traditional kernel functions that compute neighborhood graphs e.g finding the optimal number of
L2182@P50: nearest neighbors. We address these challenges by proposing spatial context driven manifold learning methods. Empirically, the
L2183@P50: study reveals that use of spatial contextual information has a bearing on the structure of the graph Laplacian that in turn links
L2184@P50: image pixel observations to their manifold spaces. Further experimental results demonstrate an improvement in the classification
L2185@P50: performance compared to traditional manifold learning methods.
L2186@P50: DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION OF HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGERY WITH SPARSE AND COLLABORATIVE GRAPHS
L2187@P50: Nam Ly, Qian Du, James E. Fowler and Nicolas Younan,
L2188@P50: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Mississippi State University, USA
L2189@P50: Abstract : Hyperspectral image dimensionality reduction with graph-based approaches is considered. With available
L2190@P50: labeled samples, a graph can be formed with these samples by constructing an affinity matrix through their sparse or collaborative
L2191@P50: representations. In addition, sparse or collaborative representation can be done using within-class samples, resulting in blocksparse representation, although within each block the representation can be either sparse or non-sparse (collaborative). The experimental results show that the block-sparse plus within-block-collaborative representation can yield the best performance.

L2195@P51: CLASSIFICATION OF HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGERY ON EMBEDDED GRASSMANNIANS
L2196@P51: Sofya Chepushtanova and Michael Kirby,
L2197@P51: Department of Mathematics, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado USA
L2198@P51: Abstract : We propose an approach for capturing the signal variability in hyperspectral imagery using the framework
L2199@P51: of the Grassmann manifold. Labeled points from each class are sampled and used to form abstract points on the Grassmannian.
L2200@P51: The resulting points on the Grassmannian have representations as orthonormal matrices and as such do not reside in Euclidean
L2201@P51: space in the usual sense. There are a variety of metrics which allow us to determine a distance matrices that can be used to realize
L2202@P51: the Grassmannian as an embedding in Euclidean space. We illustrate that we can achieve an approximately isometric embedding
L2203@P51: of the Grassmann manifold using the chordal metric while this is not the case with geodesic distances. However, non-isometric
L2204@P51: embeddings generated by using a pseudometric on the Grassmannian lead to the best classification results. We observe that as
L2205@P51: the dimension of the Grassmannian grows, the accuracy of the classification grows to 100% on two illustrative examples. We also
L2206@P51: observe a decrease in classification rates if the dimension of the points on the Grassmannian is too large for the dimension of the
L2207@P51: Euclidean space. We use sparse support vector machines to perform additional model reduction. The resulting classifier selects a
L2208@P51: subset of dimensions of the embedding without loss in classification performance.
L2209@P51: MULTI-FEATURE BASED LABEL PROPAGATION FOR SEMI-SUPERVISED CLASSIFICATION OF HYPERSPECTRAL DATA
L2210@P51: Andong Ma, Faculty of Information Engineering, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, China
L2211@P51: Li Ma, Faculty of Mechanical and Electronic Information Engineering, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, China
L2212@P51: Abstract : For hyperspectral remote sensing, some spatial features e.g., texture and morphological feature, have been successfully employed for classification task. In this paper, we investigate the utilization of multiple features in label propagation (LP)
L2213@P51: classifier, attempting to improve the classification accuracy with small size samples. The graph of LP classifier is constructed by
L2214@P51: using multiple features, where each feature calculates a similarity matrix and a composite similarity matrix is obtained via linear
L2215@P51: combination. To weight the importance of each feature in the combination, leave-one- out strategy is applied to obtain a suitable
L2216@P51: weight for each feature. Experimental results on two high resolution hyperspectral data show that the proposed approach obtained
L2217@P51: better classification performance than LP classifier with single spectral feature and LP with equal weighted multi-feature.
L2218@P51: VI. Session wed-o-2-a : Detecting difficult targets in hyperspectral imagery
L2219@P51: PROGRESS IN DETECTOR FUSION
L2220@P51: Alan Schaum, US Naval Research Laboratory
L2221@P51: Abstract : Introduced to the hyperspectral imaging community in the WHISPERS 2010 Reykjavik meeting, the “clairvoyant fusion” methodology for creating detection algorithms has since been applied to a variety of binary decision problems.
L2222@P51: These are summarized here. For any detection problem amenable to a fusion approach, an infinity of “flavors” can be devised. This
L2223@P51: paper describes what problems have been formulated in ways that insure closed form solutions. Such solutions are necessary in all
L2224@P51: applications that fuse a continuum of tests, because otherwise an infinity of logical operations would need to be implemented. The
L2225@P51: applications have featured a variety of subspace detection problems of varying dimensionality, along with several types of elliptically contoured distributions. Model subtleties not recognized by classical methods are discussed, along with a recent theoretical
L2226@P51: extension enabling the design of unbeatable methods.

L2232@P52: A FAMILY OF KERNEL ANOMALY CHANGE DETECTORS
L2233@P52: Nathan Longbotham, DigitalGlobe Longmont, CO, USA
L2234@P52: Gustavo Camps-Valls, Image Processing Lab (IPL) Universitat de València, Spain
L2235@P52: Abstract : This paper introduces the nonlinear extension of the anomaly change detection algorithms in based on the
L2236@P52: theory of reproducing kernels. The presented methods generalize their linear counterparts, under both the Gaussian and elliptically-contoured assumptions, and produce both improved detection accuracies and reduced false alarm rates. We study the
L2237@P52: Gaussianity of the data in Hilbert spaces with kernel dependence estimates, provide low-rank kernel versions to cope with the
L2238@P52: high computational cost of the methods, and give prescriptions about the selection of the kernel functions and their parameters.
L2239@P52: We illustrate the performance of the introduced kernel methods in both pervasive and anomalous change detection problems
L2240@P52: involving both real and simulated changes in multi- and hyperspectral imagery. Excellent performance is achieved in terms of
L2241@P52: detection accuracy, especially when few training examples are available. Results also reveal that the elliptically-contoured assumption may be still valid in Hilbert spaces, particularly when high pervasive distortions mask anomalous targets.
L2242@P52: TATISTICAL MOMENTS BASED METHODS FOR DETECTING SUB-PIXEL TARGET TRACKS IN LARGE IMAGE SEQUENCES
L2243@P52: Christoph C. Borel and David J. Bunker, Dept. of Eng. Physics, Air Force Institute of Technology, WPAFB, OH, USA
L2244@P52: Lori A. Mahoney, National Geospatial Intelligence Agency, WPAFB, OH, USA
L2245@P52: Abstract : This paper reviews and compares the performance of several methods to detect target tracks in image sequences. The targets are assumed to be sub-pixel or not resolved by the imaging system, and moving over a static background. To
L2246@P52: process the resulting large amount of data requires simple, fast and robust processing methods to quickly find and display tracks
L2247@P52: of moving targets in a single image. An object moving through a pixel in a scene will momentarily perturb the pixel intensity
L2248@P52: signal, introducing a change of both skewness and kurtosis in the intensity histogram relative to an undisturbed pixel. Numerical
L2249@P52: experiments show that for Gaussian and Poisson distributed system noise higher order moments (>2) perform better than second
L2250@P52: order detectors.
L2251@P52: ADVANTAGES AND LIMITATIONS OF SEGMENTATION FOR POINT TARGET DETECTION IN HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGERY
L2252@P52: Sapir Ben-Yakar, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Beer-Sheva, Israel
L2253@P52: Dan G. Blumberg, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Dept. of Geography and Environmental Development, Beer-Sheva, Israel
L2254@P52: Stanley R. Rotman, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Beer-Sheva, Israel
L2255@P52: Abstract : Segmentation appears to be an attractive preprocessing state when performing point target detection in hyperspectral data. Nevertheless, the literature contains examples of both successful and unsuccessful segmentation. Using simulations and several new analytical tools, we propose to derive guidelines when segmentation would be useful and when it would be
L2256@P52: superfluous. A real dataset with parameters when segmentation is worthwhile and when not is given.
L2257@P52: HYPERSPECTRAL ANOMALY DETECTION BASED ON A NON-UNIFORM PARTITION OF THE PIXEL
L2258@P52: Edisanter Lo, Susquehanna University Department of Mathematical Sciences Selinsgrove, U.S.A.
L2259@P52: Abstract : Detection of anomalous objects is an important application of hyperspectral imaging in remote sensing. Current anomaly detection algorithms for a subspace target are based on partialling out the main background from each spectral
L2260@P52: component of a pixel. This paper proposes an anomaly detection algorithm that partials out the main background from each subset of a pixel that has been partitioned using non-uniform subsets. The anomaly detector is defined as the Mahalanobis distance
L2261@P52: of the resulting residual. Experimental results show that the anomaly detector has a substantial improvement in detection over
L2262@P52: the conventional anomaly detectors.

L2268@P53: TITAN’S SURFACE AND ATMOSPHERE AS SEEN BY THE VIMS HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGER ONBOARD CASSINI
L2269@P53: Sébastien Rodriguez, Laboratoire AIM, Université Paris 7, CNRS UMR-7158, CEA-Saclay/DSM/IRFU/SAp, France
L2270@P53: Stéphane Le Mouélic, Laboratoire de Planétologie et Géodynamique, Université de Nantes, CNRS, UMR-6112, France
L2271@P53: Christophe Sotin, Laboratoire de Planétologie et Géodynamique, Université de Nantes, CNRS, UMR-6112, France

L2273@P53: Thomas Cornet, ESA, Madrid, Spain
L2274@P53: Jason W. Barnes, Department of Physics, University of Idaho, Engineering-Physics Building, Moscow, ID 83844, USA
L2275@P53: Robert H. Brown, Lunar and Planetary Lab., University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
L2276@P53: Abstract : The surface of Titan, the largest icy moon of Saturn, is veiled by a very thick and hazy atmosphere. The Visual
L2277@P53: and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer onboard the Cassini spacecraft, in orbit around Saturn since July 2004, conducts an intensive
L2278@P53: survey of Titan with the objective to understand the complex nature of the atmosphere and surface of this mysterious moon, and
L2279@P53: the way they interact. We review in this paper our long-term monitoring of Titan’s surface and atmosphere with the VIMS instrument. We focus on the global mapping of Titan cloud cover and geological units, and discuss the challenging problem of the
L2280@P53: decorrelation between atmospheric and surface components.
L2281@P53: VISIBLE TO NEAR-INFRARED HYPERSPECTRAL MEASUREMENTS OF MERCURY: CHALLENGES FOR DECIPHERING SURFACE MINERALOGY
L2282@P53: Rachel L. Klima and Noam R. Izenberg, The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD 20723, USA
L2283@P53: Gregory M. Holsclaw, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO 80303, USA
L2284@P53: Jörn Helbert and Mario D’Amore, Institute for Planetary Research, DLR, Berlin, Germany
L2285@P53: William E. McClintock, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO 80303, USA
L2286@P53: Sean C. Solomon, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, NY 10964, USA
L2287@P53: Department of Terrestrial Magnetism, Carnegie Institution of Washington, Washington, DC 20015, USA
L2288@P53: Abstract : The surface of Mercury has long been known to be low in ferrous iron. Spectral reflectance data from the
L2289@P53: MESSENGER spacecraft do not show a ferrous absorption band near 1 μm, complicating mineralogical analysis of Mercury’s
L2290@P53: surface. With careful calibration, however, these data can yield new constraints on the maximum amount of ferrous iron that can
L2291@P53: be present in the silicates.
L2292@P53: SPECTRAL PROPERTIES OF ICY SATURNIAN SATELLITES DERIVED FROM CASSINI DATA
L2293@P53: K. Stephan, DLR, Institute of Planetary Research, Berlin, Germany
L2294@P53: R. Jaumann, DLR, Institute of Planetary Research, Berlin, Germany and FU Berlin, Germany
L2295@P53: R. Wagner, DLR, Institute of Planetary Research, Berlin, Germany
L2296@P53: R.N. Clark, U.S.G.S., Denver, USA
L2297@P53: D.P. Cruikshank and C. Dalle Ore, NASA Ames, Moffett Field, USA
L2298@P53: R.H. Brown, UoA, Tucson, USA
L2299@P53: B. Giese, DLR, Institute of Planetary Research, Berlin, Germany
L2300@P53: T. Roatsch, DLR, Institute of Planetary Research, Berlin, Germany
L2301@P53: D. Matson, JPL, Pasadena, USA
L2302@P53: K. Baines, SSEC, Madison, USA
L2303@P53: G. Filiacchione and F. Cappacione, INAF-IASF, Rome, Italy
L2304@P53: B.J. Buratti, JPL, Pasadena, USA
L2305@P53: P.D. Nicholson, Cornell Univ., Ithaca, USA
L2306@P53: Abstract : Cassini’s Visual and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIMS) offers the first spatially resolved hyperspectral
L2307@P53: data of the Saturnian satellites allowing a detailed comparison of their spectral properties including their spatial distribution
L2308@P53: across the satellite’s surface. Additionally, images acquired by the Cassini ISS cameras offer the opportunity to study any relationships between the spectral variations to geological and morphological surface features. This is essential to understand the origin
L2309@P53: of the major and especially minor surface compounds and/or their physical properties. Either, the derived spectral variations are
L2310@P53: closely related to the surface geology of the specific satellite, or they can be explained by the interaction of the surface material and
L2311@P53: the space environment (including the planets magnetosphere). Thus, the analysis of the icy satellites spectral properties not only
L2312@P53: further our understanding of the icy satellites evolution but also complete our view about the whole planetary system.

L2323@P54: Abstract : At 525 km in mean diameter, Vesta is the second largest object of the main asteroid belt. The Visible and
L2324@P54: InfraRed (VIR) spectrometer onboard Dawn provided more than 20 millions spectra at variable spatial resolution, allowing one
L2325@P54: to discriminate the different lithologies on Vesta. In this work, we tested linear spectral unmixing on three different mixtures, to
L2326@P54: verify the applicability of linear unmixing to VIR data of Vesta, and to determine the accuracy of the detection of the amount of
L2327@P54: the different minerals. We studied the following mixtures: two pyroxenes, pyroxene and olivine, and pyroxene and plagioclase. We
L2328@P54: next applied linear spectral unmixing to VIR spectra for localized features and larger areas, with the goal of deriving the composition and abundance of the minerals present.
L2329@P54: A PRELIMINARY RESEARCH ON QUANTITATIVE RETRIEVAL OF HYDROUS MINERALS AROUND THE MARS
L2330@P54: SCIENCE LABORATORY LANDING SITE
L2331@P54: Tong Shuai and Xia Zhang, State Key Laboratory of Remote Sensing Sciences, Institute of Remote Sensing and Digital
L2332@P54: Earth, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100101, China
L2333@P54: Abstract : The detection of hydrous minerals is of great importance in revealing the early water environment and even
L2334@P54: biotic activities on Mars. However, few studies focus on quantitatively retrieving hydrous minerals due to some problems. In this
L2335@P54: paper, the area around the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) landing site is studied for quantitatively retrieving hydrous minerals.
L2336@P54: Firstly, the distribution of hydrous minerals is extracted using water absorption features. Then, sparse unmixing is employed with
L2337@P54: CRISM spectral library to retrieve the abundance of hydrous minerals in the hydrous region. The results show that seven hydrous
L2338@P54: minerals are quantitatively retrieved, e.g. actinolite, montmorillonite, saponite, jarosite and so forth, and the total concentration
L2339@P54: of all hydrous minerals can reach up to 40% near the lower reaches of Mount Sharp.
